t: Relation Extraction Engine: a plain-language overview
title: Relation Extraction Engine: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Relation Extraction Engine does and why archives need it. A relation extraction engine reads sentences and pulls out the relationships inside them: who did what to whom. 'Edison founded Menlo Park' becomes the triple (Edison, founded, Menlo Park). Thousands of sentences become a web of facts a computer can query, count, and graph.
demo:
# Relation Extraction Engine - runnable demo (JAH-ATK167-000001)
import re
RANK = 1
SIG = False
SENTS = ['Edison founded Menlo Park.', 'Tesla built the first induction motor.', 'Curie did not found the institute.']
pat = re.compile(r"([A-Z][A-Za-z .'-]+?)\s+(founded|acquired|built|wrote|invented|leads|joined)\s+([A-Z][A-Za-z .'-]+?)(?:\.|$)")
triples = []
for s in SENTS:
    for m in pat.finditer(s):
        subj, pred, obj = (x.strip(" .") for x in m.groups())
        neg = "did not" in s[:m.start()].lower()[-20:]
        triples.append((subj, pred, obj, "NEGATED" if neg else "asserted"))
for t in triples:
    print("(%s) -[%s]-> (%s)" % (t[0], t[1], t[2]), "|", t[3])
if RANK >= 2:
    print("triples extracted:", len(triples), "from", len(SENTS), "sentences")
if RANK >= 3:
    from collections import Counter
    print("predicate histogram:", dict(Counter(t[1] for t in triples)))
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-REL-" + "JAH-ATK167-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK167-000001", "OK")
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Relation Extraction Engine works
title: How the Relation Extraction Engine works
description: Overview: what the Relation Extraction Engine does and why archives need it. Real engines extract subject-verb-object triples using dependency parses (spaCy, Stanford CoreNLP): the parser finds the verb, its nominal subject, and its object, then normalizes each side to canonical entity forms. Open information extraction systems (OpenIE, ReVerb) use part-of-speech patterns to catch relations the dependency rules miss, and distant supervision trains classifiers on known facts to label new sentences. Each triple carries its source sentence and a confidence score, and near-duplicate triples are merged by entity and predicate normalization.

t: How the Relation Extraction Engine works: the deep tour
title: How the Relation Extraction Engine works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Relation Extraction Engine does and why archives need it. Real engines extract subject-verb-object triples using dependency parses (spaCy, Stanford CoreNLP): the parser finds the verb, its nominal subject, and its object, then normalizes each side to canonical entity forms. Open information extraction systems (OpenIE, ReVerb) use part-of-speech patterns to catch relations the dependency rules miss, and distant supervision trains classifiers on known facts to label new sentences. Each triple carries its source sentence and a confidence score, and near-duplicate triples are merged by entity and predicate normalization. Advanced extraction handles n-ary relations (who sold what to whom for how much), negation ('did not found'), and modality ('might acquire') — all of which flip or weaken a triple's meaning and must be recorded as qualifiers. Quality is measured by triple precision and recall against human-annotated corpora. The limits are implicit relations, metaphor, and long-range references across paragraphs; the engine marks low-confidence triples for review instead of asserting them, because a wrong triple poisons every query built on it.

# Relation Extraction Engine - runnable demo (JAH-ATK167-000014)
import re
RANK = 2
SIG = False
SENTS = ['Ada wrote the first algorithm.', 'Bell invented the telephone.']
pat = re.compile(r"([A-Z][A-Za-z .'-]+?)\s+(founded|acquired|built|wrote|invented|leads|joined)\s+([A-Z][A-Za-z .'-]+?)(?:\.|$)")
triples = []
for s in SENTS:
    for m in pat.finditer(s):
        subj, pred, obj = (x.strip(" .") for x in m.groups())
        neg = "did not" in s[:m.start()].lower()[-20:]
        triples.append((subj, pred, obj, "NEGATED" if neg else "asserted"))
for t in triples:
    print("(%s) -[%s]-> (%s)" % (t[0], t[1], t[2]), "|", t[3])
if RANK >= 2:
    print("triples extracted:", len(triples), "from", len(SENTS), "sentences")
if RANK >= 3:
    from collections import Counter
    print("predicate histogram:", dict(Counter(t[1] for t in triples)))
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-REL-" + "JAH-ATK167-000014")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK167-000014", "OK")

title: The Relation Extraction Engine at archive scale
description: Production: how the Relation Extraction Engine runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real engines extract subject-verb-object triples using dependency parses (spaCy, Stanford CoreNLP): the parser finds the verb, its nominal subject, and its object, then normalizes each side to canonical entity forms. Open information extraction systems (OpenIE, ReVerb) use part-of-speech patterns to catch relations the dependency rules miss, and distant supervision trains classifiers on known facts to label new sentences. Each triple carries its source sentence and a confidence score, and near-duplicate triples are merged by entity and predicate normalization. Advanced extraction handles n-ary relations (who sold what to whom for how much), negation ('did not found'), and modality ('might acquire') — all of which flip or weaken a triple's meaning and must be recorded as qualifiers. Quality is measured by triple precision and recall against human-annotated corpora. The limits are implicit relations, metaphor, and long-range references across paragraphs; the engine marks low-confidence triples for review instead of asserting them, because a wrong triple poisons every query built on it.
